rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Commentators connect human origin from dust both to Adam and to food animals and milk: plants nourish them, and plants grow from dust, making human bodies physically dust-derived.
rows.anchor: Commentators see this verse as a reference not only to the fact that Adam

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The drop is understood as semen, as in the description of seed as base fluid.
rows.anchor: The drop is often understood to refer to semen (R)

rows.speaker: commentators (R, Ṭ)
rows.claim: Formed and unformed flesh is generally taken to mean that some pregnancies reach term while others miscarry before a fully formed human being results; the appointed term is seen as indicating this.
rows.anchor: while others miscarry before producing fully formed human beings (R, Ṭ).

words: وَنُقِرُّ فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ مَا نَشَآءُ إِلَىٰٓ أَجَلٍۢ مُّسَمًّۭى
rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Commentators cite a hadith describing 40 nights as a drop, then 40 as a clot, then 40 as a lump; an angel records provision, deeds, lifespan, and whether the person will be wretched or joyous.
rows.anchor: some commentators mention a ḥadīth that states, “Your creation is such that you are brought together in your mother’s belly

words: وَمِنكُم مَّن يُتَوَفَّىٰ وَمِنكُم مَّن يُرَدُّ إِلَىٰٓ أَرْذَلِ ٱلْعُمُرِ
rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: Some die before old age, while the most abject life is weakness and loss of faculties in old age; the verse resembles other descriptions of declining strength and knowledge.
rows.anchor: the most abject life refers to the weakness and loss of faculties one experiences in old age (IK).

rows.speaker: Some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators say faith's strength can spare people the infirmities and weakness of old age.
rows.anchor: Some commentators argue that people can be spared the infirmities and weaknesses of old age in accordance with the strength of their faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḥaqq may be rendered God is the Truth or God is the Real/Reality.
rows.anchor: could also be rendered,“God is the Real/Reality.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The revival of vegetation from dry earth is a recurring Quranic symbol for resurrection, linked to several passages describing dead land made alive.
rows.anchor: The growth of vegetation from dry earth is a common symbol in the Quran for the resurrection of the dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The entire created world prostrates, not only human beings; the Quran also describes worship by beings other than angels and humans.
rows.anchor: The prostrating of the whole created world, not just human beings, is also mentioned in 13:15

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Prostration denotes both physical action and the humble state of worship that the action signifies.
rows.anchor: Prostration signifies not only the physical action, but also the very state of humble worship that prostration suggests (R).

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: The punishment having come due means that it is deserved.
rows.anchor: The punishment has come due means that it is deserved (Ṭ).

words: وَمَن يُهِنِ ٱللَّهُ فَمَا لَهُۥ مِن مُّكْرِمٍ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The structure that none can ennoble whom God disgraces parallels statements about God's guidance, help, and abandonment.
rows.anchor: The structure of Whomsoever God disgraces, none can ennoble is similar to such other Quranic statements

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse recalls believers expelled from Makkah for their faith, a frequently cited grievance of the Muslim community against Quraysh.
rows.anchor: The expulsion of the believers from their homes in Makkah, mentioned also in 2:191, 217, 246; 3:195

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers were permitted to use force in response to persecution and expulsion for professing that God is their Lord.
rows.anchor: The believers were given permission to use force because of the wrongs committed against them: persecution and being forced to leave because of their faith

words: لَوْلَا دَفْعُ ٱللَّهِ ٱلنَّاسَ بَعْضَهُم بِبَعْضٍۢ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repelling force is justified because it prevents destruction of different houses of worship; by implication, defense applies in similar future circumstances involving actual expulsion and potential destruction.
rows.anchor: By implication, such defense or “repelling” should take place in the future under similar conditions

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Monasteries are usually understood as houses of Christian monks.
rows.anchor: Monasteries renders ṣawāmiʿ, usually understood to be houses of Christian monks

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some also associate the monasteries with the Sabeans.
rows.anchor: but also associated by some with the Sabeans

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Churches are generally understood to be Christian houses of worship.
rows.anchor: churches renders biyaʿ, which most have understood to refer to Christian houses of worship

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Churches may alternatively refer to Jewish temples.
rows.anchor: but which may also refer to Jewish temples

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Synagogues are usually understood as Jewish houses of worship.
rows.anchor: synagogues renders ṣalawāt, usually understood to mean Jewish houses of worship

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some link the synagogues with the Sabeans.
rows.anchor: but linked by some with the Sabeans (see 2:62)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Masājid literally means places of prostration and is generally associated with Muslim houses of worship.
rows.anchor: mosques renders masājid, a word meaning “place of prostrations” and associated by most commentators with the houses of worship of Muslims themselves

rows.speaker: another opinion
rows.claim: An alternate view takes masājid as a general term for the three preceding kinds of houses of worship.
rows.anchor: although another opinion sees masājid as a general term referring to the previous three types of houses of worship (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: many commentators and jurists
rows.claim: Commentators and jurists who hold Islam supersedes earlier religions take the verse to concern pre-Islamic houses of worship.
rows.anchor: For many commentators and jurists, in keeping with their general theory of Islam’s supersession

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims are prohibited from damaging or destroying treaty communities' houses of worship both within and beyond Islamic lands.
rows.anchor: Muslims, however, are prohibited from damaging or destroying the houses of worship belonging to peoples with whom there is a treaty

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Those who help God are understood to be those who help God's religion and His Prophet.
rows.anchor: Those who help Him is understood to mean those who help God’s religion and His Prophet (Q, R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mansak, rendered rite, can denote either a ritual act or a place of ritual significance.
rows.anchor: can mean both a ritual act and a place of ritual significance

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation advises the Prophet and, by extension, believers not to debate members of other communities about these questions.
rows.anchor: Let them not argue with thee is understood to mean that the Prophet, and by extension all believers, should not engage in debate

rows.speaker: some commentators (R)
rows.claim: An alternative interpretation tells disputants to stop arguing with Muslims and embrace Islam.
rows.anchor: although some understand this to mean that those who would argue with the Muslims should themselves stop their dispute and embrace Islam (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If disputes continue, believers should leave judgment to God's knowledge and final judgment in the Hereafter rather than expect religious differences to be settled in this world.
rows.anchor: If the disputants continue, the believers are to remind them of God’s Knowledge and that God will judge the differences between religions

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The drop is seminal fluid.
rows.anchor: The drop refers to seminal fluid

rows.speaker: R, Ṭ
rows.claim: The secure dwelling place is the womb.
rows.anchor: the secure dwelling place is the womb (R, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clot and lump of flesh refer to the stages of physical human growth, discussed in the commentary on 22:5–6.
rows.anchor: On the blood clot and lump of flesh, see 22:5–6c, which also discusses the stages of the physical growth of human beings.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: One interpretation is that the spirit is breathed into what previously existed only as a form.
rows.anchor: Brought him into being as another creation is interpreted variously as the inbreathing of the spirit into what was previously only a form (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Another interpretation takes the phrase to mean the act of being born.
rows.anchor: the act of being born (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: A further interpretation is development into mature adulthood and full realization of one's faculties.
rows.anchor: one’s development into mature adulthood and the full realization of one’s faculties (Q, R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb rendered smite can also mean burn or scorch.
rows.anchor: Smite renders a verb that also means “to burn or scorch.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other passages describe the Fire or punishment appearing on human faces.
rows.anchor: Other verses that contain a description of the Fire

rows.speaker: some commentators (Q, Ṭ)
rows.claim: Some explain the grimace as the flames disfiguring the lips.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, the grimace results from the disfigurement of the lips by the flames (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: some commentators (Ṭ)
rows.claim: Inquiring may mean signaling one's presence by clearing the throat or knocking, so occupants know someone is there before being greeted.
rows.anchor: Some say inquire and greet the dwellers refers to a signal like clearing one’s throat or knocking at the door

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: The greeting is the formula Peace be upon you.
rows.anchor: The greeting here is the formula “Peace be upon you”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The disbelievers mock the choice of Muhammad and his followers rather than themselves by God.
rows.anchor: On the disbelievers’ incredulity regarding God’s choice of Muhammad and his followers instead of them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mocking prophets is a recurring trait attributed to disbelievers, as illustrated by earlier prophets and multiple other passages.
rows.anchor: The mockery carried out by the disbelievers is a common trait ascribed to them

rows.speaker: Aj, Z
rows.claim: Idolaters obey their passions so fully that they worship them.
rows.anchor: The idolaters obey their passions to the point of worshipping them (Aj, Z).

rows.speaker: some commentators (Aj, Q, R)
rows.claim: Some report that fickle idolaters would abandon an idol for another they found better or more beautiful.
rows.anchor: some were so fickle that, upon seeing a better or more beautiful idol than the one they were worshipping, they would quickly abandon the first

rows.speaker: Aj, Q
rows.claim: Those ruled by impulse and passion cannot be persuaded by the Prophet to worship the One God.
rows.anchor: those who act on impulse and respond to their passions cannot be persuaded to worship the One God (Aj, Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse connects with the reminder that the Prophet is not a warder over them.
rows.anchor: See also 88:22: Thou art not a warder over them.

rows.speaker: Ṭ
rows.claim: Karīm can mean good and beautiful; the verse concerns vegetation that people and animals can eat.
rows.anchor: also means good and beautiful

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Kind can include growth that seems beneficial and growth whose benefit is not apparent; every growing thing has some benefit, though people may not know it.
rows.anchor: notes that kind here can refer to both what is beneficial

rows.speaker: Sufyān al-Thawrī
rows.claim: A saying attributed to Sufyān al-Thawrī calls humans growths of the earth: those entering the Garden are noble, while those entering the Fire are wretched.
rows.anchor: Another meaning of growth appears in a saying attributed to Sufyān al-Thawrī

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zawj can also mean pair.
rows.anchor: Kind renders zawj, which also means “pair.”

rows.speaker: Su
rows.claim: Read as pair, the verse may refer to Adam and Eve, the most noble pair, ancestors of all prophets and saints.
rows.anchor: the verse can be understood as a reference to Adam and Eve, “the most noble pair,” who gave rise to all the prophets and saints (Su).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fuller account has Moses see a distant fire on the mountain, approach it, speak with God, and receive the mission to go to Pharaoh.
rows.anchor: Moses’ initial call is mentioned in greater detail in 20:9–48 and 28:29–35

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: One reading has God command Moses to ask the people whether they will not be reverent.
rows.anchor: Some understand this verse to mean that God is commanding Moses to ask them, “Will you not be reverent?” (Q).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Depending on the vocalization, the phrase can instead ask whether they will reverence God.
rows.anchor: Depending on how the end of this verse is vocalized, it could also mean, “Will they not reverence Me?” (R).

rows.speaker: some commentators (Ṭ)
rows.claim: Reverence connotes mindfulness or caution; here it can mean being mindful of the Hereafter's punishment.
rows.anchor: and thus some understand this verse to mean that they should be mindful of the punishment of the Hereafter (Ṭ).

rows.speaker: Q, Ṭ
rows.claim: Some take Pharaoh's kāfir as disbeliever in relation to Pharaoh's own religion.
rows.anchor: some interpret this to mean that Pharaoh is calling Moses a disbeliever with respect to Pharaoh’s religion (Q, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: some commentators (Th)
rows.claim: Some reject a theological reading of kufr, arguing that Pharaoh was not motivated by such theological concerns.
rows.anchor: Some commentators dismiss the idea that Pharaoh would take a position on disbelief

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāfir can mean ingrate, one who covers over a received blessing; here it refers to what Pharaoh gave Moses while he lived among the Egyptians.
rows.anchor: Kāfir means ingrate (cf. 2:276; 31:32; 43:15) insofar as it connotes the “covering over” of a blessing one received from another

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The phrase may be adverbial, meaning that Moses killed the Egyptian while in a state of ingratitude.
rows.anchor: while you were an ingrate,” meaning that the act of killing the Egyptian was done in that state (R).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Noah narrative is also related in several other Quranic passages, including Sūrah 71.
rows.anchor: For the story of Noah, also see 7:59–64; 10:71–73; 11:25–48;

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Although Noah is singular, his people's denial of him implies rejection of all messengers because the path to recognizing a messenger is universal across history, and each messenger calls people to affirm all messengers.
rows.anchor: the people’s denial of him would include the rejection of all messengers, since the path to recognizing and affirming a messenger is universal

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: Another interpretation is that they rejected Noah's prophecy that messengers would come after him.
rows.anchor: a category stands for a specific individual (Q)

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: A further explanation is that the plural category of messengers stands for Noah as a specific individual.
rows.anchor: or it may be an example in which a category stands for a specific individual (Q).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Calling Noah their brother means that he belonged to their people.
rows.anchor: Their brother means that he was one of them (R).

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: Taqwā here can mean being mindful or careful, specifically avoiding disobedience toward God.
rows.anchor: Here being reverent is also interpreted as being mindful or careful, meaning, “Will you not be mindful of disobedience toward Me?” (R).

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: Noah was trustworthy because his people had known him throughout his life and had no reason to mistrust him, just as Muhammad was known among Quraysh; he had always been truthful.
rows.anchor: Noah was trustworthy because being one of his people, he was known to them all his life, just as Muhammad was among the Quraysh

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: The call to reverence God comes before obedience to Noah because obedience depends on reverence.
rows.anchor: The call to reverence God precedes the call to obey Noah, because the latter depends upon the former (R).

rows.speaker: Q
rows.claim: The people were to obey Noah when he called them to faith.
rows.anchor: The people were to obey Noah when he enjoined them to faith (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly presents messengers as seeking no enrichment or status for delivering the message of faith.
rows.anchor: A common theme in the Quran is that the messengers do not seek enrichment or status in return for being instrumental in bringing the message of faith

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clear-warner phrase is also used of Noah in several passages and of Muhammad in many others.
rows.anchor: This phrase is also attributed to Noah in 7:184; 11:25; 71:2 as well as to the Prophet Muhammad in 15:89; 22:49;

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A warner (nadhīr) is often paired with a bearer of glad tidings (bashīr).
rows.anchor: often combined with being bringers of glad tidings

rows.speaker: Q, R
rows.claim: The disbelievers threaten to stone Noah to death for denigrating their gods and religion.
rows.anchor: The disbelievers say they will stone Noah to death (R) for denigrating their gods and their religion (Q).

rows.speaker: some commentators (Q, Ṭ)
rows.claim: Some take stoned to mean abuse and vilification rather than literal stoning, as in Satan called al-rajīm, usually understood as accursed.
rows.anchor: but abuse and vilification (Q, Ṭ), as in the phrase

rows.speaker: al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Qurṭubī cites Abraham's father's threat in 19:46 as an example where stoning is metaphorical rather than literal.
rows.anchor: Al-Qurṭubī points to the example of “stoning” in the words spoken by Abraham’s father to him in 19:46

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The five opening verses of Hūd's story follow the same pattern as Noah's and the stories of later prophets.
rows.anchor: These five verses form a pattern that opens the story of Noah and each of the prophets who follow

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening of Ṣāliḥ's story repeats the pattern used for other prophets, as discussed for Noah.
rows.anchor: For a similar opening to other prophets’ stories, cf. vv. 105–9, 123–27, 160–64, 176–80.
